newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Melzer says inflation hurts payments system.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Melzer says inflation hurts payments system.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President Thomas Melzer said on Friday that even low inflation could hurt the efficiency of the payments system and noted that the connection should be worrisome for the Fed.

"Inflation affects the payments system by distorting private incentives so that payments are carried out in ways that are socially costly," he told a seminar on banking and the Internet sponsored by Kentucky's Murray State University.
A copy of the speech was made available to Reuters in Washington.
"This is because inflation can drive a wedge between private benefits and the actual cost to society of using a particular payment form," he added.

Melzer defined electronic money and payments -- which include debit and ATM cards -- as any electronic form of access to a payment instrument or the payment instrument itself, if it exists in electronic form.
He said that new forms of electronic money would not compromise the Fed's ability to conduct monetary policy and control inflation.
But Melzer did single out two forms of electronic payments -- sweep accounts and stored-value cards -- which he said highlight how inflation can interfere with the role money plays in the economy.

Sweep accounts, or computer programs operated by banks to "sweep" customer deposit balances back and forth between various types of deposit accounts, can save banks money by reducing the dollars they hold in demand deposit accounts, and against which they are required to hold non-earning reserves.
Melzer said such accounts represented "a real cost to society with no net gain."

"The savings reaped by banks, in terms of reduced holdings of non-earning reserve balances or vault cash, are completely offset from society's point of view by reduced Fed earnings, which ultimately belong to the taxpayer," Melzer said.
In order to solve this problem, he said the Fed could, if permitted by law, pay interest on reserve balances, decreasing the incentive for institutions to try to reduce these balances.
He also said that if the Fed moved to an environment of long-term price stability such methods of economizing on money holdings would fade into insignificance.
Melzer also questioned the benefit of stored-value cards, which he likened to electronic traveler's checks.
"It appears to me that the economics of stored-value cards depend heavily on collecting an interest rate spread that varies directly with the rate of inflation," he said.
He cited both electronic payment forms as examples where inflation was creating "opportunities for private gain at the expense of other parties that are unable or unwilling to defend themselves."
"The economy as a whole, and the payments system in particular, could operate even more efficiently if price stability were achieved and sustained," Melzer concluded.
